bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw material price volatility - PVC and CPVC resin — Named first among the operational risks in Astral's own Risk Management table. The MD&A shows why it is structural rather than incidental: FY26 split into two distinct phases, with much of the year spent in a low-price PVC environment after extended global oversupply and weak feedstock pricing, then a sharp increase in PVC resin prices in the later part of the year on Middle East geopolitical tensions, supply-chain disruption and changed global trade flows, which triggered widespread channel restocking. India still depends on imports for a significant portion of its PVC and CPVC resin requirement, so realisations, inventory value and working capital all swing with a price the company does not set. Stated mitigations: strategic sourcing relationships, diversified sourcing channels, long-term supplier agreements, leveraging backward integration, better inventory planning for critical materials, and timely price interventions.
- Intensifying market competition and constrained pricing power — Listed as a risk in the Risk Management table. The MD&A corroborates it in the newer verticals: in paints the operating environment 'remained highly competitive as both established players and new entrants intensified investments in channel expansion, dealer incentives and brand-building initiatives', industry pricing power stayed constrained despite stable demand and favourable input costs, and lower realisations plus downtrading within product categories weighed on revenue growth, with the decorative segment experiencing limited pricing power all year. This bears directly on the businesses Astral is spending most heavily to scale. Stated mitigations: product differentiation through innovation and value-added solutions, expanding distribution reach and brand equity, and operational efficiency and cost optimisation.
- Supply chain disruption — A named risk in the Risk Management table, and one the MD&A shows materialising during FY26: geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, supply-chain disruptions and shifts in global trade flows drove the late-year resin price spike. It compounds the import dependence for PVC and CPVC resin and reaches a manufacturing base spread over 21 units in three countries. Stated mitigations: a diversified supplier base across geographies, enhanced supply-chain visibility and risk monitoring, strategic inventory reserves, and stronger local sourcing wherever feasible.
- Capacity expansion and project execution risk — Explicitly named in the Risk Management table, and the live exposure for a company mid-build: the Kanpur facility was commissioned and Hyderabad continued ramping during FY26, the Khambhat unit is still under development, and the backward-integration CPVC resin project through Nexelon Chem has yet to deliver. Delay, cost overrun or a slow ramp on any of these defers the volume and margin benefit the company is counting on. Stated mitigations: structured project management and governance processes for new facilities and capacity additions, and close monitoring of project milestones to ensure timely execution, cost discipline and operational readiness.
- Talent acquisition and retention — Named in the Risk Management table and echoed in the BRSR materiality table, which identifies talent management as requiring competitive benefits, clear career development and a positive work environment. It matters structurally for a business scaling several new verticals at once - paints, bathware and construction chemicals - where execution depends on building sales, technical and plant teams faster than the core business ever needed to. Stated mitigations: a high-performance and inclusive work environment, investment in employee development and leadership pipelines, competitive compensation and benefits, and structured training and career growth programmes.
- Regulatory and compliance risk — Named in the Risk Management table. Astral manufactures in India, the UK and the USA, sells into 40 export markets, and operates in a category governed by tightening BIS compliance requirements and product certification standards - the MD&A itself cites stricter BIS compliance as one of the forces shifting the market from unorganised to organised players, which cuts both ways as an obligation and an advantage. The BRSR materiality table separately flags corporate governance as a risk where poor governance leads to legal issues and loss of confidence. Stated mitigations: robust compliance frameworks and governance mechanisms, and continuous monitoring of regulatory developments with timely corrective action.
- Product quality and safety — Named in the Risk Management table, and material because Astral's competitive case rests on branded, certified product in categories where failure is expensive and visible - potable water distribution, sewage management, industrial piping and fire protection networks. The BRSR materiality table separately identifies occupational health and safety as a risk carrying legal liability, employee downtime and reputational damage. Stated mitigations: stringent quality management systems, testing protocols and certification standards, plus periodic audits and continuous strengthening of quality assurance across manufacturing facilities.
- Cybersecurity and data privacy — Named in the Risk Management table and independently flagged in the BRSR materiality table, where the rationale given is that data breaches can lead to legal penalties and loss of customer trust. The exposure grows with the company's digital ESG transformation programme, expanding modern-trade and digital sales channels, and a distribution system spanning over 3,990 distributors and 2.7 lakh dealers. Stated mitigations: advanced cybersecurity infrastructure, monitoring systems and incident response capabilities, regular security audits, and employee awareness and data-protection training.

- Advanced polymer technologies and specialised applications - the integration of Al-Aziz has enhanced capabilities in specialised fittings and polyolefin-based solutions, opening opportunities across utility, infrastructure and industrial applications.
- Premiumisation and value-added product mix - continued investment in differentiated platforms such as FirePro (UL/FM-approved fire sprinkler piping), Silencio low-noise drainage, Power Drain surface drainage, OPVC and PEX to build position in higher-value segments.
- Scaling emerging verticals - paints (built on Astral Paints plus Gem Paints), bathware and construction chemicals are being developed as new growth platforms through portfolio enhancement, market expansion and distribution development.
- Geographic distribution deepening, especially rural - the adhesives network reaches over 13,000 towns with a roadmap to 20,000 towns, supported by the recently launched New Bharat initiative to accelerate rural market development.
- Paints geographic roll-out toward Pan-India presence - having entered 6 states, the company plans to add more states shortly with the eventual aim of becoming a Pan-India company.
- Decentralised manufacturing - bringing production closer to markets to improve supply-chain agility, enhance customer service levels and reduce logistical complexity and dependence on individual geographies and logistics corridors.
- Leveraging an integrated business model - using a common distribution ecosystem across multiple product categories to create synergies, deepen customer engagement and expand share of wallet across the construction value chain; the ability to scale new businesses through an established platform is called a key driver of growth in the years ahead.
- International expansion - restructuring and improved operational discipline in the UK, integration of advanced hybrid sealant technology acquired from Switzerland, leveraging US manufacturing for niche industrial and specialised applications, and a newly established local office in the UAE to extend the global footprint in plumbing and adhesives.
- Brand building at scale - nationwide consumer campaigns such as Bondtite with Ranbir Kapoor to enhance visibility and engagement across key markets.
- Investment in product authentication technologies, advanced manufacturing capabilities and specialised product platforms to create durable competitive advantages.
- Sustainability embedded as a growth imperative - expanding renewable energy, advancing a digital ESG transformation journey for data collection, monitoring and reporting, and pursuing green certification for products.
- Disciplined capital allocation and risk management - every major investment evaluated through a long-term lens balancing growth potential with financial prudence and risk-adjusted returns, to maintain a strong balance sheet and preserve financial flexibility; forward focus stated as profitable growth, disciplined capital allocation, prudent risk management and efficient execution of strategic investments.
- Working capital discipline - sustained focus on working capital efficiency so that growth is supported by healthy cash generation and disciplined resource deployment.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Astral operates 21 manufacturing units across India, the United Kingdom and the United States with a total production capacity of approximately 5,97,089 metric tonnes per annum. The company describes a deliberate strategy of expanding and decentralising its manufacturing footprint - locating production units near key demand centres to cut logistics complexity, improve supply-chain reliability and service regional markets faster. During FY26 the Kanpur facility was commissioned and the Hyderabad facility continued to ramp up; management describes FY26 as the year in which several years of capacity investment moved 'from development phase to active value creation', with these recent expansions in Hyderabad and Kanpur plus continued development of regional facilities improving service responsiveness and reducing logistics cost. Work continued on the upcoming Khambhat manufacturing unit, which was not yet commissioned at year end and for which no commissioning date, capacity or cost is stated in this bundle. In the plumbing business, installed capacity was raised 9.34% during the year, from 3,81,957 MT to 4,17,645 MT, while sales volume rose from 2,27,090 MT to 2,63,026 MT; the Directors' Report states the company incurred capital expenditure of Rs 3,284 million during FY26 towards plant and machineries, factory building and other capital expenditure. Expansion also came inorganically: the Board approved the acquisition of 100% of Al-Aziz Plastics Private Limited on 17 April 2025, expected to strengthen the plastic pipes and fittings business through product portfolio diversification and additional manufacturing capacities, and on 11 August 2025 approved the acquisition of 80% of Nexelon Chem Private Limited as a backward-integration initiative enabling the company to manufacture CPVC resin in-house to support cost optimisation, supply-chain efficiency and margin enhancement. The Board also approved buying out the remaining 5% of Seal It Services Limited (UK) and the 20% minority in Astral Chemie Limited (formerly Astral Coatings Private Limited), making both wholly owned subsidiaries. On the international side, Astral started an office in Dubai to support the export trajectory of the adhesives business. Management flags ongoing investment in capacity, product development and distribution expansion for the adhesives and sealants business, and long-term potential from backward-integration initiatives. On energy, the company reports 7MW of renewable energy and a reduced carbon footprint. No rupee quantum for any individual project, no project-level capacity addition and no commissioning timeline for Khambhat or the CPVC resin project appears anywhere in this bundle.

outlook.body:
- Government water and housing programmes are the largest demand catalyst - Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0, PM Awas Yojana and PM Krishi Sinchai Yojana continue to expand India's water and sanitation infrastructure; as of June 2026 over 15.8 crore rural households had tap-water connections under JJM versus about 3.2 crore at launch in 2019.
- Union Budget FY26 allocated Rs 67,000 crore to the Jal Jeevan Mission and over Rs 70,000 crore to Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana; FY27 allocations cited are JJM Rs 67,670 crore, PMKSY Rs 6,587 crore, Ministry of Jal Shakti total Rs 94,808 crore and central capital expenditure Rs 12.2 lakh crore.
- Raw-material price volatility was the defining feature of FY26 - a low-price PVC environment for much of the year following global oversupply and weak feedstock pricing, then a sharp rise in PVC resin prices in the latter part of the year on Middle East geopolitical tensions, supply-chain disruption and changed global trade flows, which triggered widespread channel restocking and improved industry realisations.
- Organised manufacturers continue to gain market share, because stronger balance sheets, wider distribution reach and superior inventory management let them navigate raw-material volatility better than smaller regional players.
- Premiumisation of Indian housing - a gradual shift toward premium and mid-premium residential development is driving higher adoption of CPVC plumbing, acoustic drainage, fire protection piping and advanced water management technologies.
- Import substitution in resin - India still imports a significant portion of its PVC and CPVC resin requirement, but domestic resin manufacturing and backward integration projects underway across the industry are expected to improve supply security, reduce import dependence, support long-term margin stability and reduce working capital requirement.
- Plastic pipe industry outlook favourable - industry volumes expected to grow 7.5%-8%, with organised players likely to outperform on stronger brands, wider distribution and certified portfolios; the next phase of growth driven by specialised and value-added categories such as CPVC, HDPE, PEX, fire protection systems and advanced drainage.
- Adhesives and sealants - the Indian market is expected to register volume growth of about 8-10% in FY27, driven by construction activity, renovation demand and growing rural consumption; growth led by waterproofing systems, tile-fixing solutions, repair and rehabilitation products, industrial bonding technologies and sustainable formulations.
- The UK adhesives market is expected to remain under macroeconomic pressure though early signs of stabilisation are visible, while export opportunities across the Middle East, Africa and Europe remain strong.
- Adhesives end-market breadth - construction and infrastructure (waterproofing, tile adhesives, repair mortars, grouts, sealants), packaging boosted by organised retail, e-commerce, quick commerce and flexible packaging (hot melt, pressure sensitive and laminating adhesives), and manufacturing momentum in automotive, appliances, electronics and engineered products driving industrial adhesive demand.
- Adhesives mix shift to specialised, technology-driven formulations - water-based adhesives, polyurethane systems, hybrid sealants and low-VOC products gaining prominence on environmental standards and customer preference, and typically offering higher performance and improved profitability than conventional products.
- Paints - the Indian paints and coatings industry was valued at about Rs 93,000 crore in 2025 and is projected to reach Rs 1.46 lakh crore by 2030 (IBEF); decorative accounts for nearly three-fourths of demand. FY26 demand improved in the second half on housing completions, festive demand and stronger rural consumption, particularly in Tier II and Tier III markets, but lower realisations and downtrading weighed on revenue growth and the decorative segment had limited pricing power all year.
- Paints structural drivers - India's construction sector grew 8.4% in FY26; expanding housing stock, infrastructure build-up driving protective coatings and waterproofing, consumer preference for premium and differentiated finishes, and faster-than-category growth in waterproofing and surface protection expanding the addressable market. Competitive intensity remains elevated as established players and new entrants invest in channel expansion, dealer incentives and brand building.
- Bathware / sanitaryware - the India bath fittings market is expected to rise from USD 11.49 billion in 2025 to USD 12.36 billion in 2026 and reach USD 17.97 billion by 2031, a CAGR of 7.8% over 2026-2031. FY26 was a recovery year after a subdued FY25, with support from residential developments, commercial real estate and hospitality projects and acceleration in the second half as housing completions picked up; PMAY-U 2.0 supported the housing ecosystem.
- Bathware drivers - urbanisation, premiumisation of lifestyle, water efficiency and sustainability awareness (dual flush, low-flow faucets, aerators, sensor-based fittings), green building standards, replacement demand as consumers upgrade bathrooms, and investment in hotels, hospitals, educational institutions, airports and commercial developments.
- Astral-specific outperformance claim - in paints the company says it continued to outperform the broader industry through strong brand equity, extensive distribution, product innovation and execution, delivering healthy growth and gaining market share across key categories; management also states it gained market share across most product categories in FY26 as prior-year investments in manufacturing, product development, brand building and distribution began translating into a stronger market position.
- Margin lever from backward integration - the captive 40,000 MT CPVC resin project is expected to improve volumes and margins on CPVC pipes and fittings from FY28 and reduce import dependence and currency exposure.
- Working capital lever - the working capital cycle improved from 37 days to 24 days during FY26 and receivable days improved.
- Bathware - growing traction across both retail and project segments has resulted in a project pipeline that is increasing very fast, which management says reinforces confidence in the long-term potential of the business.
- Plumbing - Power Drain surface drainage systems are now being deployed in landmark projects including the Narendra Modi stadium and the Dharamshala stadium.
- FirePro - the fire protection business recorded a significant increase in sales during FY26, reflecting increasing adoption of UL/FM-approved certified fire sprinkler piping systems across commercial applications.

deepdive.thesis: Astral Limited delivered resilient double-digit EBITDA growth despite severe PVC inventory losses and forex headwinds, driven by strategic expansion into high-margin adjacent businesses like sanitaryware, valves, and adhesives, with strong execution on channel expansion and brand building. The company is repositioning as a holistic building solutions provider, leveraging its distribution network and brand equity to capture market share in underpenetrated segments.

open.item: Management expects polymer prices to remain elevated after a year of sharp volatility, following the late-FY26 spike in PVC resin prices driven by Middle East geopolitical tensions and supply-chain disruption.

Astral will be the first company to start PVC manufacturing in India through a captive 40,000 MT plant, reducing import dependence and currency exposure, with volume and margin benefits on CPVC pipes and fittings expected from FY28.

Astral is developing captive CPVC resin manufacturing through Nexelon Chem - a captive 40,000 MT project that will make it the only CPVC pipe manufacturer in India producing its own resin, expected to improve volumes and margins on CPVC pipes and fittings from FY28.
Astral is continuing progress on its upcoming Khambhat manufacturing unit, having commissioned the Kanpur facility during FY26.
Through the acquisition of 80% of Nexelon Chem Private Limited, Astral intends to manufacture CPVC resin in-house to support cost optimisation, supply-chain efficiency and margin enhancement.

Astral aims to make its newer verticals - paints, bathware and construction materials - increasingly meaningful contributors to long-term growth, with the paints focus now shifting to distribution expansion, product mix and operational efficiency as initial market development is largely established.

Astral is expanding its international business - exporting to more than 40 countries, opening an office in Dubai / UAE and participating in international trade shows including ISH Frankfurt, Big 5 Dubai, Big 5 Saudi and Big 5 South Africa - to diversify revenue streams over the long term.
The adhesives network reaches over 13,000 towns across India today, with a clear roadmap to reach 20,000 towns in the next few years, supported by the New Bharat rural initiative.

risks.note: Named first among the operational risks in Astral's own Risk Management table. The MD&A shows why it is structural rather than incidental: FY26 split into two distinct phases, with much of the year spent in a low-price PVC environment after extended global oversupply and weak feedstock pricing, then a sharp increase in PVC resin prices in the later part of the year on Middle East geopolitical tensions, supply-chain disruption and changed global trade flows, which triggered widespread channel restocking. India still depends on imports for a significant portion of its PVC and CPVC resin requirement, so realisations, inventory value and working capital all swing with a price the company does not set. Stated mitigations: strategic sourcing relationships, diversified sourcing channels, long-term supplier agreements, leveraging backward integration, better inventory planning for critical materials, and timely price interventions.
risks.risk: Raw material price volatility - PVC and CPVC resin

risks.note: Listed as a risk in the Risk Management table. The MD&A corroborates it in the newer verticals: in paints the operating environment 'remained highly competitive as both established players and new entrants intensified investments in channel expansion, dealer incentives and brand-building initiatives', industry pricing power stayed constrained despite stable demand and favourable input costs, and lower realisations plus downtrading within product categories weighed on revenue growth, with the decorative segment experiencing limited pricing power all year. This bears directly on the businesses Astral is spending most heavily to scale. Stated mitigations: product differentiation through innovation and value-added solutions, expanding distribution reach and brand equity, and operational efficiency and cost optimisation.
risks.risk: Intensifying market competition and constrained pricing power

risks.note: A named risk in the Risk Management table, and one the MD&A shows materialising during FY26: geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, supply-chain disruptions and shifts in global trade flows drove the late-year resin price spike. It compounds the import dependence for PVC and CPVC resin and reaches a manufacturing base spread over 21 units in three countries. Stated mitigations: a diversified supplier base across geographies, enhanced supply-chain visibility and risk monitoring, strategic inventory reserves, and stronger local sourcing wherever feasible.

Explicitly named in the Risk Management table, and the live exposure for a company mid-build: the Kanpur facility was commissioned and Hyderabad continued ramping during FY26, the Khambhat unit is still under development, and the backward-integration CPVC resin project through Nexelon Chem has yet to deliver. Delay, cost overrun or a slow ramp on any of these defers the volume and margin benefit the company is counting on. Stated mitigations: structured project management and governance processes for new facilities and capacity additions, and close monitoring of project milestones to ensure timely execution, cost discipline and operational readiness.
risks.risk: Capacity expansion and project execution risk

risks.note: Named in the Risk Management table and echoed in the BRSR materiality table, which identifies talent management as requiring competitive benefits, clear career development and a positive work environment. It matters structurally for a business scaling several new verticals at once - paints, bathware and construction chemicals - where execution depends on building sales, technical and plant teams faster than the core business ever needed to. Stated mitigations: a high-performance and inclusive work environment, investment in employee development and leadership pipelines, competitive compensation and benefits, and structured training and career growth programmes.

Named in the Risk Management table. Astral manufactures in India, the UK and the USA, sells into 40 export markets, and operates in a category governed by tightening BIS compliance requirements and product certification standards - the MD&A itself cites stricter BIS compliance as one of the forces shifting the market from unorganised to organised players, which cuts both ways as an obligation and an advantage. The BRSR materiality table separately flags corporate governance as a risk where poor governance leads to legal issues and loss of confidence. Stated mitigations: robust compliance frameworks and governance mechanisms, and continuous monitoring of regulatory developments with timely corrective action.

Named in the Risk Management table, and material because Astral's competitive case rests on branded, certified product in categories where failure is expensive and visible - potable water distribution, sewage management, industrial piping and fire protection networks. The BRSR materiality table separately identifies occupational health and safety as a risk carrying legal liability, employee downtime and reputational damage. Stated mitigations: stringent quality management systems, testing protocols and certification standards, plus periodic audits and continuous strengthening of quality assurance across manufacturing facilities.

Named in the Risk Management table and independently flagged in the BRSR materiality table, where the rationale given is that data breaches can lead to legal penalties and loss of customer trust. The exposure grows with the company's digital ESG transformation programme, expanding modern-trade and digital sales channels, and a distribution system spanning over 3,990 distributors and 2.7 lakh dealers. Stated mitigations: advanced cybersecurity infrastructure, monitoring systems and incident response capabilities, regular security audits, and employee awareness and data-protection training.

currentContext.expansion: Astral operates 21 manufacturing units across India, the United Kingdom and the United States with a total production capacity of approximately 5,97,089 metric tonnes per annum. The company describes a deliberate strategy of expanding and decentralising its manufacturing footprint - locating production units near key demand centres to cut logistics complexity, improve supply-chain reliability and service regional markets faster. During FY26 the Kanpur facility was commissioned and the Hyderabad facility continued to ramp up; management describes FY26 as the year in which several years of capacity investment moved 'from development phase to active value creation', with these recent expansions in Hyderabad and Kanpur plus continued development of regional facilities improving service responsiveness and reducing logistics cost. Work continued on the upcoming Khambhat manufacturing unit, which was not yet commissioned at year end and for which no commissioning date, capacity or cost is stated in this bundle. In the plumbing business, installed capacity was raised 9.34% during the year, from 3,81,957 MT to 4,17,645 MT, while sales volume rose from 2,27,090 MT to 2,63,026 MT; the Directors' Report states the company incurred capital expenditure of Rs 3,284 million during FY26 towards plant and machineries, factory building and other capital expenditure. Expansion also came inorganically: the Board approved the acquisition of 100% of Al-Aziz Plastics Private Limited on 17 April 2025, expected to strengthen the plastic pipes and fittings business through product portfolio diversification and additional manufacturing capacities, and on 11 August 2025 approved the acquisition of 80% of Nexelon Chem Private Limited as a backward-integration initiative enabling the company to manufacture CPVC resin in-house to support cost optimisation, supply-chain efficiency and margin enhancement. The Board also approved buying out the remaining 5% of Seal It Services Limited (UK) and the 20% minority in Astral Chemie Limited (formerly Astral Coatings Private Limited), making both wholly owned subsidiaries. On the international side, Astral started an office in Dubai to support the export trajectory of the adhesives business. Management flags ongoing investment in capacity, product development and distribution expansion for the adhesives and sealants business, and long-term potential from backward-integration initiatives. On energy, the company reports 7MW of renewable energy and a reduced carbon footprint. No rupee quantum for any individual project, no project-level capacity addition and no commissioning timeline for Khambhat or the CPVC resin project appears anywhere in this bundle.

risks.risk: Raw material price volatility - PVC and CPVC resin
risks.note: Named first among the operational risks in Astral's own Risk Management table. The MD&A shows why it is structural rather than incidental: FY26 split into two distinct phases, with much of the year spent in a low-price PVC environment after extended global oversupply and weak feedstock pricing, then a sharp increase in PVC resin prices in the later part of the year on Middle East geopolitical tensions, supply-chain disruption and changed global trade flows, which triggered widespread channel restocking. India still depends on imports for a significant portion of its PVC and CPVC resin requirement, so realisations, inventory value and working capital all swing with a price the company does not set. Stated mitigations: strategic sourcing relationships, diversified sourcing channels, long-term supplier agreements, leveraging backward integration, better inventory planning for critical materials, and timely price interventions.

risks.risk: Intensifying market competition and constrained pricing power
risks.note: Listed as a risk in the Risk Management table. The MD&A corroborates it in the newer verticals: in paints the operating environment 'remained highly competitive as both established players and new entrants intensified investments in channel expansion, dealer incentives and brand-building initiatives', industry pricing power stayed constrained despite stable demand and favourable input costs, and lower realisations plus downtrading within product categories weighed on revenue growth, with the decorative segment experiencing limited pricing power all year. This bears directly on the businesses Astral is spending most heavily to scale. Stated mitigations: product differentiation through innovation and value-added solutions, expanding distribution reach and brand equity, and operational efficiency and cost optimisation.

A named risk in the Risk Management table, and one the MD&A shows materialising during FY26: geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, supply-chain disruptions and shifts in global trade flows drove the late-year resin price spike. It compounds the import dependence for PVC and CPVC resin and reaches a manufacturing base spread over 21 units in three countries. Stated mitigations: a diversified supplier base across geographies, enhanced supply-chain visibility and risk monitoring, strategic inventory reserves, and stronger local sourcing wherever feasible.

risks.risk: Capacity expansion and project execution risk
risks.note: Explicitly named in the Risk Management table, and the live exposure for a company mid-build: the Kanpur facility was commissioned and Hyderabad continued ramping during FY26, the Khambhat unit is still under development, and the backward-integration CPVC resin project through Nexelon Chem has yet to deliver. Delay, cost overrun or a slow ramp on any of these defers the volume and margin benefit the company is counting on. Stated mitigations: structured project management and governance processes for new facilities and capacity additions, and close monitoring of project milestones to ensure timely execution, cost discipline and operational readiness.

Named in the Risk Management table and echoed in the BRSR materiality table, which identifies talent management as requiring competitive benefits, clear career development and a positive work environment. It matters structurally for a business scaling several new verticals at once - paints, bathware and construction chemicals - where execution depends on building sales, technical and plant teams faster than the core business ever needed to. Stated mitigations: a high-performance and inclusive work environment, investment in employee development and leadership pipelines, competitive compensation and benefits, and structured training and career growth programmes.

Named in the Risk Management table. Astral manufactures in India, the UK and the USA, sells into 40 export markets, and operates in a category governed by tightening BIS compliance requirements and product certification standards - the MD&A itself cites stricter BIS compliance as one of the forces shifting the market from unorganised to organised players, which cuts both ways as an obligation and an advantage. The BRSR materiality table separately flags corporate governance as a risk where poor governance leads to legal issues and loss of confidence. Stated mitigations: robust compliance frameworks and governance mechanisms, and continuous monitoring of regulatory developments with timely corrective action.

Named in the Risk Management table, and material because Astral's competitive case rests on branded, certified product in categories where failure is expensive and visible - potable water distribution, sewage management, industrial piping and fire protection networks. The BRSR materiality table separately identifies occupational health and safety as a risk carrying legal liability, employee downtime and reputational damage. Stated mitigations: stringent quality management systems, testing protocols and certification standards, plus periodic audits and continuous strengthening of quality assurance across manufacturing facilities.

Named in the Risk Management table and independently flagged in the BRSR materiality table, where the rationale given is that data breaches can lead to legal penalties and loss of customer trust. The exposure grows with the company's digital ESG transformation programme, expanding modern-trade and digital sales channels, and a distribution system spanning over 3,990 distributors and 2.7 lakh dealers. Stated mitigations: advanced cybersecurity infrastructure, monitoring systems and incident response capabilities, regular security audits, and employee awareness and data-protection training.

one-line thesis: Astral Limited delivered resilient double-digit EBITDA growth despite severe PVC inventory losses and forex headwinds, driven by strategic expansion into high-margin adjacent businesses like sanitaryware, valves, and adhesives, with strong execution on channel expansion and brand building. The company is repositioning as a holistic building solutions provider, leveraging its distribution network and brand equity to capture market share in underpenetrated segments.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Astral Limited, founded in 1996 as a piping solutions business, is an Indian building-materials group operating across nine categories with 21 manufacturing units in India, the UK and the USA and a total production capacity of 5,97,089 MT per annum.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Astral manufactures and sells building materials spanning plastic piping systems and fittings, water tanks, adhesives and sealants, construction chemicals, paints, bathware, specialised valves, specialised fittings and infrastructure solutions. Its products serve plumbing, sewerage and drainage, agriculture, industrial, fire-protection and urban-infrastructure applications across residential, commercial, industrial and infrastructure end markets. The company reaches customers through one of the industry's most extensive distribution networks - over 3,990 distributors and more than 2.7 lakh dealers spanning over 20,000 towns in India - and exports to more than 40 countries.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Government water and housing programmes are the largest demand catalyst - Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0, PM Awas Yojana and PM Krishi Sinchai Yojana continue to expand India's water and sanitation infrastructure; as of June 2026 over 15.8 crore rural households had tap-water connections under JJM versus about 3.2 crore at launch in 2019.
- Union Budget FY26 allocated Rs 67,000 crore to the Jal Jeevan Mission and over Rs 70,000 crore to Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana; FY27 allocations cited are JJM Rs 67,670 crore, PMKSY Rs 6,587 crore, Ministry of Jal Shakti total Rs 94,808 crore and central capital expenditure Rs 12.2 lakh crore.
- Raw-material price volatility was the defining feature of FY26 - a low-price PVC environment for much of the year following global oversupply and weak feedstock pricing, then a sharp rise in PVC resin prices in the latter part of the year on Middle East geopolitical tensions, supply-chain disruption and changed global trade flows, which triggered widespread channel restocking and improved industry realisations.
- Organised manufacturers continue to gain market share, because stronger balance sheets, wider distribution reach and superior inventory management let them navigate raw-material volatility better than smaller regional players.
- Premiumisation of Indian housing - a gradual shift toward premium and mid-premium residential development is driving higher adoption of CPVC plumbing, acoustic drainage, fire protection piping and advanced water management technologies.
- Import substitution in resin - India still imports a significant portion of its PVC and CPVC resin requirement, but domestic resin manufacturing and backward integration projects underway across the industry are expected to improve supply security, reduce import dependence, support long-term margin stability and reduce working capital requirement.
- Plastic pipe industry outlook favourable - industry volumes expected to grow 7.5%-8%, with organised players likely to outperform on stronger brands, wider distribution and certified portfolios; the next phase of growth driven by specialised and value-added categories such as CPVC, HDPE, PEX, fire protection systems and advanced drainage.
- Adhesives and sealants - the Indian market is expected to register volume growth of about 8-10% in FY27, driven by construction activity, renovation demand and growing rural consumption; growth led by waterproofing systems, tile-fixing solutions, repair and rehabilitation products, industrial bonding technologies and sustainable formulations.
- The UK adhesives market is expected to remain under macroeconomic pressure though early signs of stabilisation are visible, while export opportunities across the Middle East, Africa and Europe remain strong.
- Adhesives end-market breadth - construction and infrastructure (waterproofing, tile adhesives, repair mortars, grouts, sealants), packaging boosted by organised retail, e-commerce, quick commerce and flexible packaging (hot melt, pressure sensitive and laminating adhesives), and manufacturing momentum in automotive, appliances, electronics and engineered products driving industrial adhesive demand.
- Adhesives mix shift to specialised, technology-driven formulations - water-based adhesives, polyurethane systems, hybrid sealants and low-VOC products gaining prominence on environmental standards and customer preference, and typically offering higher performance and improved profitability than conventional products.
- Paints - the Indian paints and coatings industry was valued at about Rs 93,000 crore in 2025 and is projected to reach Rs 1.46 lakh crore by 2030 (IBEF); decorative accounts for nearly three-fourths of demand. FY26 demand improved in the second half on housing completions, festive demand and stronger rural consumption, particularly in Tier II and Tier III markets, but lower realisations and downtrading weighed on revenue growth and the decorative segment had limited pricing power all year.
- Paints structural drivers - India's construction sector grew 8.4% in FY26; expanding housing stock, infrastructure build-up driving protective coatings and waterproofing, consumer preference for premium and differentiated finishes, and faster-than-category growth in waterproofing and surface protection expanding the addressable market. Competitive intensity remains elevated as established players and new entrants invest in channel expansion, dealer incentives and brand building.
- Bathware / sanitaryware - the India bath fittings market is expected to rise from USD 11.49 billion in 2025 to USD 12.36 billion in 2026 and reach USD 17.97 billion by 2031, a CAGR of 7.8% over 2026-2031. FY26 was a recovery year after a subdued FY25, with support from residential developments, commercial real estate and hospitality projects and acceleration in the second half as housing completions picked up; PMAY-U 2.0 supported the housing ecosystem.
- Bathware drivers - urbanisation, premiumisation of lifestyle, water efficiency and sustainability awareness (dual flush, low-flow faucets, aerators, sensor-based fittings), green building standards, replacement demand as consumers upgrade bathrooms, and investment in hotels, hospitals, educational institutions, airports and commercial developments.
- Astral-specific outperformance claim - in paints the company says it continued to outperform the broader industry through strong brand equity, extensive distribution, product innovation and execution, delivering healthy growth and gaining market share across key categories; management also states it gained market share across most product categories in FY26 as prior-year investments in manufacturing, product development, brand building and distribution began translating into a stronger market position.
- Margin lever from backward integration - the captive 40,000 MT CPVC resin project is expected to improve volumes and margins on CPVC pipes and fittings from FY28 and reduce import dependence and currency exposure.
- Working capital lever - the working capital cycle improved from 37 days to 24 days during FY26 and receivable days improved.
- Bathware - growing traction across both retail and project segments has resulted in a project pipeline that is increasing very fast, which management says reinforces confidence in the long-term potential of the business.
- Plumbing - Power Drain surface drainage systems are now being deployed in landmark projects including the Narendra Modi stadium and the Dharamshala stadium.
- FirePro - the fire protection business recorded a significant increase in sales during FY26, reflecting increasing adoption of UL/FM-approved certified fire sprinkler piping systems across commercial applications.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Astral operates 21 manufacturing units across India, the United Kingdom and the United States with a total production capacity of approximately 5,97,089 metric tonnes per annum. The company describes a deliberate strategy of expanding and decentralising its manufacturing footprint - locating production units near key demand centres to cut logistics complexity, improve supply-chain reliability and service regional markets faster. During FY26 the Kanpur facility was commissioned and the Hyderabad facility continued to ramp up; management describes FY26 as the year in which several years of capacity investment moved 'from development phase to active value creation', with these recent expansions in Hyderabad and Kanpur plus continued development of regional facilities improving service responsiveness and reducing logistics cost. Work continued on the upcoming Khambhat manufacturing unit, which was not yet commissioned at year end and for which no commissioning date, capacity or cost is stated in this bundle. In the plumbing business, installed capacity was raised 9.34% during the year, from 3,81,957 MT to 4,17,645 MT, while sales volume rose from 2,27,090 MT to 2,63,026 MT; the Directors' Report states the company incurred capital expenditure of Rs 3,284 million during FY26 towards plant and machineries, factory building and other capital expenditure. Expansion also came inorganically: the Board approved the acquisition of 100% of Al-Aziz Plastics Private Limited on 17 April 2025, expected to strengthen the plastic pipes and fittings business through product portfolio diversification and additional manufacturing capacities, and on 11 August 2025 approved the acquisition of 80% of Nexelon Chem Private Limited as a backward-integration initiative enabling the company to manufacture CPVC resin in-house to support cost optimisation, supply-chain efficiency and margin enhancement. The Board also approved buying out the remaining 5% of Seal It Services Limited (UK) and the 20% minority in Astral Chemie Limited (formerly Astral Coatings Private Limited), making both wholly owned subsidiaries. On the international side, Astral started an office in Dubai to support the export trajectory of the adhesives business. Management flags ongoing investment in capacity, product development and distribution expansion for the adhesives and sealants business, and long-term potential from backward-integration initiatives. On energy, the company reports 7MW of renewable energy and a reduced carbon footprint. No rupee quantum for any individual project, no project-level capacity addition and no commissioning timeline for Khambhat or the CPVC resin project appears anywhere in this bundle.

hero.oneLiner: Astral Limited, founded in 1996 as a piping solutions business, is an Indian building-materials group operating across nine categories with 21 manufacturing units in India, the UK and the USA and a total production capacity of 5,97,089 MT per annum.
